content.title: AMOC - Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation | CMEMS
content.text: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) acts as an ocean conveyor belt, transporting warm water northward from the tropics across the Atlantic at the surface, and cold water southward at the bottom. This circulation is driven by differences in temperature and salinity, which create differences in water density – a process known as thermohaline circulation.In the North Atlantic Ocean, the warm water cools and becomes denser, sinking and down into the deep ocean. This dense water then travels southward along the ocean floor, eventually warming and resurfacing to complete the cycle. This loop distributes heat around the planet – the AMOC accounts for around 90% of the total northward ocean heat transport across the Atlantic Ocean – and is an important component of Earth's climate.The Gulf Stream is the largest current in the North Atlantic Ocean, transporting approximately 30 billion kilograms of water per second northward along the eastern coast of North America. This warm current carries water that can be 5°C to 15°C warmer than surrounding waters, releasing significant amounts of thermal energy to the atmosphere and surrounding ocean as it flows. The Gulf Stream is formed by the combination of the AMOC and a second major circulation pattern – the North Atlantic Subtropical Gyre caused by Earth's rotation, which concentrates the flow on the western side of the Atlantic basin and is two to ten times larger than the AMOC component. The merger of these two phenomena creates the powerful Gulf Stream current.Is the AMOC really responsible for the climate in Europe?Take New York and Porto, for example. Even though they’re at about the same latitude, New York sees temperatures ranging from -2.2°C in winter to 29.5°C in summer, while Porto’s temperatures are much milder, going from 5°C to 26°C.This smaller seasonal difference in Porto is mainly due to the influence of the Atlantic Ocean. As winds travel over the ocean, they exchange heat with the water - warming the air in winter and cooling it in summer - which helps keep the climate in Western Europe more stable.The Atlantic Ocean’s warm waters are fed by the Gulf Stream and also act as a heat reservoir. During summer, the ocean stores vast amounts of heat. In winter, this stored heat is released into the atmosphere and carried eastward by prevailing westerly winds. This creates Europe's characteristically mild winters and cool summers.Will the Gulf Stream collapse and cause a colder climate in western Europe?Our climate is changing, and climate models predict that the AMOC will slow down during the 21st century. The primary cause is freshwater input into the North Atlantic from melting ice. Since 1993, Greenland's melting ice sheet has added around 5,000 km³ of freshwater into the subpolar North Atlantic Ocean. As the waters of the North Atlantic warm, they also mix with this melting ice, becoming less salty and therefore less dense. This lighter water sinks more slowly, weakening the mechanism that drives the AMOC.Despite past significant changes during transitions between ice ages, the AMOC has remained stable for 8,000 years. However, continued global warming poses a real threat to this circulation system. Computer models consistently project that the AMOC will weaken over the coming centuries, with some showing slowing even within this century.The decline of the AMOC will not shut down the Gulf Stream completely but will induce a decrease in its warm water transport. This decrease could lead to a significant cooling of north-western Europe (-2-3°C), despite global warming. A shift in precipitation patterns and a sea level rise along the US East Coast would be observed.
